statements.markdown:
At $s\in S\cap(0,1)$, the function $G$ has an interior minimum of
value zero. Thus $G'(s)=0$ and $G''(s)\ge0$, giving
$$
q(s)=s,\qquad q'(s)\le1.
$$
If $0\in S$, the argument needs the zero-field initial condition in
addition to the one-sided minimum. We have $G(0)=0$ and $q(0)=0$, so
$$
G(h)=G(0)+\int_0^h(t-q(t))\,dt
     =\frac12(1-q'(0))h^2+o(h^2).
$$
Nonnegativity for $h>0$ implies $q'(0)\le1$. This works whether or not
zero is an atom. The equality $q(0)=0$ comes from symmetry, rather than
from differentiating a one-sided minimum. If $0\notin S$, no condition
$G(0)=0$ has been obtained or used.

G'(s)=s-q(s)=0,\qquad G''(s)=1-q'(s)\geq0,

$q(0)=0$ independently. Consequently

same slope bound at zero.

statements.markdown:
We need information about $q$ at the ends of a possible gap. An
interior support point $s$ is a minimum of $G$. Since
$G'(s)=s-q(s)$ and $G''(s)=1-q'(s)$, ordinary calculus gives

$$
q(s)=s,\qquad q'(s)\le1.
$$

If zero belongs to the support, contact and symmetry give
$G(0)=q(0)=0$. Were $q'(0)>1$, continuity would give $q'(t)>1$
for small positive $t$, and integration would then give $q(t)>t$, so
$G'(t)=t-q(t)<0$. Starting from $G(0)=0$, this would force $G(t)<0$,
a contradiction. Hence $q'(0)\le1$, and this one-sided argument covers
an atom at zero.
